title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 51–52
description: Curated B2 vocabulary for quantities, degree and intensity, numerical language, shapes and arithmetic.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and exercise vocabulary; all teaching examples and notes are newly written, and original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Source teaching pages, quantity scale, shape illustrations, number-pronunciation tables, practice activities 51.1–51.5 and 52.1–52.5, and answer-key entries reviewed for central lexical and grammatical targets.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA where reasonably reliable; longer expressions omit IPA rather than supply unverified connected-speech transcriptions. Pronounceable words are used instead of bare mathematical symbols for word audio.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except natural Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared teaching pages, exercises, illustrations and answers with source; checked meaning, grammatical patterns, British usage, original examples, provenance, unique IDs and static audio fields against the canonical Units 01–02 reference. No live application import or TTS test was performed.
audit.limitations: Empty audio fields mean no bundled recordings. Actual browser TTS playback, speech recognition and VocabLab import were not tested.

units.title: Unit 51 — Number, quantity, degree and intensity
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 108–109 (PDF pages 109–110).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Distinguish number with countable nouns from amount with uncountable nouns.
Choose accurate quantity adjectives by size, register and whether a quantity is excessive.
Use informal and formal quantifiers with appropriate agreement and meaning.
Apply utter, utterly, total, totally and wholly in natural fixed collocations.

items.example: A large number of applicants attended the interview.
items.note: Use a number of with countable plural nouns, not with uncountable money.

items.example: The machine consumes a small amount of electricity.
items.note: Use an amount of with uncountable nouns; compare a number of machines.

items.example: Even a minute amount of dust can affect this sensor.
items.note: Formal adjective meaning extremely small; stress the second syllable, unlike the time unit minute.

items.example: Only a tiny amount of paint is needed for the repair.
items.note: Neutral adjective for very small quantities; less formal than minute.

items.example: Attendance this month was about average.
items.note: About average means neither particularly high nor low.

items.example: The redesign required a considerable amount of time.
items.note: Fairly formal: large enough to be important, but not necessarily excessive.

items.example: There was a significant increase in energy consumption.
items.note: Emphasises an amount or change large enough to be noticed or matter.

items.example: The company invested a substantial sum in new equipment.
items.note: Fairly formal: large or important in amount, size or value.

items.example: Excessive pressure could damage the valve.
items.note: Means too much, not merely a very large amount; often implies a problem.

items.example: A vast quantity of sand covered the road after the storm.
items.note: Emphasises very great size or extent; naturally used with amounts, areas and quantities.

items.example: An enormous amount of data was collected overnight.
items.note: Very large in amount or size; does not by itself mean too much.

items.example: A large number of volunteers joined the project.
items.note: Follow with a plural countable noun; the verb is normally plural when referring to the members.

items.example: A large amount of information is stored on the server.
items.note: Follow with an uncountable noun such as information; normally takes a singular verb.

items.example: We ordered a dozen replacement screws.
items.note: A dozen means twelve; dozens of usually means many rather than an exact count.

items.example: Dozens of visitors gathered outside the museum.
items.note: Used with countable plural nouns; not normally with an uncountable noun like time.

items.example: The traditional expression a score of years means twenty years.
items.note: As a quantity noun, a score is twenty; uncommon in everyday modern counting.

items.example: Scores of residents attended the public meeting.
items.note: Means many and is often more formal than loads of; followed by plural countable nouns.

items.pt: um monte de; muita quantidade de
items.example: We still have heaps of time to finish the task.
items.note: Informal; used with countable or uncountable nouns; common in casual British English.

items.example: Don't hurry; we've got bags of time before the train.
items.note: Informal quantifier; with time it means plenty of time.

items.example: We have loads of spare connectors in the cupboard.
items.note: Informal and usable with countable or uncountable nouns; agreement depends on the noun.

items.example: There was tons of food left after the event.
items.note: Informally means a very large quantity, not necessarily a measured weight; with singular food use was.

items.pt: uma gota de; um pouquinho de (líquido)
items.example: Could you add a drop of milk to my tea?
items.note: A very small amount of liquid; a drop can be figurative rather than a measured drop.

items.example: The announcement was met with utter silence.
items.note: Strong adjective placed before nouns such as silence, chaos and nonsense; not used freely with all nouns.

items.example: That claim is utter nonsense and has no supporting evidence.
items.note: Utter naturally intensifies the noun nonsense.

items.example: The committee showed utter contempt for the safety rules.
items.note: Formal collocation meaning complete disrespect.

items.example: After the alarm stopped, the room fell into utter silence.
items.note: Utter intensifies a strong noun denoting a complete state.

items.example: The sudden change in instructions caused utter confusion.
items.note: A fixed strong collocation for a complete lack of understanding or order.

items.example: The unexpected cancellation caused utter chaos at the station.
items.note: Utter naturally modifies the noun chaos; compare utterly confused.

items.example: For a moment she felt utter despair about the setback.
items.note: Strong, somewhat dramatic collocation; commonly used in serious contexts.

items.example: The proposed deadline seemed utterly unrealistic.
items.note: Adverb used before strong adjectives; the book highlights ridiculous, confused and impossible.

items.example: It would be utterly ridiculous to ignore the test results.
items.note: Typical strong adjective collocation; not utter ridiculous.

items.example: I was utterly confused by the new registration system.
items.note: Utterly modifies an adjective; utter modifies a noun.

items.example: Finishing the entire experiment in ten minutes is utterly impossible.
items.note: Strong emphasis on impossibility.

items.example: The charity called for a total ban on the harmful substance.
items.note: As an adjective, especially natural with ban or disbelief in this unit.

items.example: She stared at the result in total disbelief.
items.note: Fixed noun collocation meaning complete inability to believe something.

items.example: The company introduced a total ban on smoking indoors.
items.note: A ban on something means an official prohibition.

items.example: The two designs are totally different.
items.note: Adverb commonly used with different, unexpected, unsuitable and wrong.

items.example: Their second proposal was totally different from the first.
items.note: Natural emphasis on contrast; different from is the standard pattern.

items.example: The invitation was totally unexpected.
items.note: Describes something not anticipated at all.

items.example: That material is totally unsuitable for outdoor use.
items.note: Unsuitable for identifies the intended purpose or situation.

items.example: The initial temperature estimate was totally wrong.
items.note: Strong rejection of an answer, view or assumption.

items.example: The decision was wholly reasonable in the circumstances.
items.note: Often slightly more formal than totally; frequent with dependent, inadequate and unacceptable.

items.example: Our timetable is wholly dependent on the delivery date.
items.note: Dependent on is the required preposition.

items.example: The original cooling system was wholly inadequate.
items.note: Strong formal criticism that something is not sufficient for its purpose.

items.example: Such a delay would be wholly unacceptable to our customers.
items.note: A strong, rather formal evaluation.

sectionsChecked: A: Number and quantity; scale and countability
B: Informal words for number and quantity; agreement
C: Degree and intensity; fixed collocations

units.title: Unit 52 — Numbers and shapes
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 110–111 (PDF pages 111–112).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Pronounce percentages, decimals, common fractions, powers, measurements and long numbers in natural British English.
Identify common two- and three-dimensional shapes and their corresponding adjectives.
Use dimension, circle and angle vocabulary precisely when describing shapes.
Say basic arithmetic operations and numerical relationships with correct grammatical forms.

items.example: Only twenty per cent of the invitations received a reply.
items.note: Standard British spelling is per cent in two words; write the numeral with a percent sign if desired.

items.example: The final reading was eight point six volts.
items.note: In English, say point for the decimal separator, not comma.

items.example: Three point seven is a decimal number.
items.note: Decimals are written with a dot in English and read digit by digit after point.

items.example: One and two thirds is greater than one and a half.
items.note: The whole-number part is joined to the fraction by and.

items.example: Four fifths of the committee voted in favour.
items.note: Fractions use an ordinal denominator, usually plural after a numerator above one.

items.example: Nine thirteenths is a little less than three quarters.
items.note: The denominator is the plural ordinal thirteenths.

items.pt: nove dividido por treze; nove sobre treze
items.example: Nine over thirteen is another way to read the fraction.
items.note: Over is an alternative way to say many fractions in mathematical contexts.

items.example: Five squared is twenty-five.
items.note: After a number, squared means raised to the power of two.

items.example: Four cubed is sixty-four.
items.note: After a number, cubed means raised to the power of three.

items.example: Two to the power of five equals thirty-two.
items.note: Used for exponents, such as four to the power of three.

items.example: The water temperature reached thirty degrees Celsius.
items.note: Say degrees for most values and one degree for exactly one.

items.example: The forecast predicted seventy degrees Fahrenheit.
items.note: Fahrenheit is a temperature scale; the expression includes degrees.

items.example: The workbench measures two metres by one metre.
items.note: In dimensions, say by between measurements; not multiplied by.

items.example: The thermometer read nought degrees Celsius.
items.note: British form of zero, especially natural for temperatures; zero is also common.

items.example: The phone number starts with oh seven.
items.note: A common pronunciation of the digit zero in telephone numbers.

items.pt: duplo; duas vezes o mesmo algarismo
items.example: She read the two consecutive eights as double eight.
items.note: Telephone numbers often use double before repeated digits.

items.example: The town has nearly one million residents.
items.note: No plural -s after an exact number: two million residents.

items.example: The auditorium can hold three thousand people.
items.note: In long numbers, group digits by thousands, using a comma as a separator.

items.example: Draw a circle around the correct option.
items.note: A two-dimensional round shape; related adjective circular.

items.example: The table has a circular top.
items.note: Adjective derived from circle.

items.example: The diagram contains a square with four equal sides.
items.note: A square has four equal sides and four right angles; the adjective is also square.

items.example: The badge features a regular pentagon.
items.note: A five-sided plane shape.

items.example: A pentagonal panel fits this decorative frame.
items.note: Adjective corresponding to pentagon.

items.example: The screen is shaped like a rectangle.
items.note: A four-sided shape with four right angles.

items.example: The office has a long rectangular window.
items.note: Adjective corresponding to rectangle.

items.example: Each support bracket forms a triangle.
items.note: A two-dimensional figure with three sides and three angles.

items.example: They placed a triangular sign beside the road.
items.note: Adjective derived from triangle.

items.example: Draw an octagon with eight equal sides.
items.note: An eight-sided plane shape.

items.example: The hall has an octagonal floor plan.
items.note: Adjective corresponding to octagon.

items.example: She drew an oval around the heading.
items.note: Both noun and adjective; roughly egg-shaped.

items.example: The two lines meet at a right angle.
items.note: A right angle measures ninety degrees.

items.example: The diameter of the circular opening is ten centimetres.
items.note: A line passing through the centre from one side of a circle to the other.

items.example: The radius of the wheel is half its diameter.
items.note: Distance from a circle's centre to its circumference; plural radii or radiuses, depending on context.

items.example: Measure the circumference of the circular tank.
items.note: The distance around a circle, or its outer boundary.

items.example: The seating area forms a semi-circle around the stage.
items.note: One of two halves formed when a circle is divided by its diameter; semicircle is also a spelling.

items.example: Draw a diagonal line between opposite corners.
items.note: Appears in exercise 52.5; a diagonal joins non-adjacent corners.

items.example: The diagram shows a right-angled triangle.
items.note: A triangle with one angle of ninety degrees, used in the drawing exercise.

items.example: The model represents the planet as a sphere.
items.note: A perfectly round three-dimensional solid.

items.example: The sensor is housed in a spherical case.
items.note: Adjective corresponding to sphere.

items.example: The wooden cube has six square faces.
items.note: Three-dimensional shape with six equal square faces; distinct from cubed for exponents.

items.example: The container has a capacity of two cubic metres.
items.note: Adjective for a cube or for volume; distinct from the exponent word cubed.

items.example: The glass roof forms a small pyramid.
items.note: A solid with a polygonal base and triangular faces meeting at a point.

items.example: The monument has a pyramidal structure.
items.note: Adjective corresponding to pyramid.

items.example: The staircase rises in a spiral.
items.note: Can name a coiling shape or describe one; appears with the 3-D illustrations.

items.example: The model divides the sphere into two hemispheres.
items.note: One half of a sphere; also used for halves of the Earth.

items.example: Addition is the first operation the children practised.
items.note: Mathematical operation indicated by the plus sign.

items.example: Subtraction gives the difference between two numbers.
items.note: Mathematical operation indicated by the minus sign.

items.example: Multiplication is useful for counting equal groups.
items.note: Mathematical operation often shown with a times sign.

items.example: Division tells us how many groups of equal size we can make.
items.note: Mathematical operation often shown with a division sign or a fraction bar.

items.example: Eight plus five equals thirteen.
items.note: Spoken name of the addition symbol.

items.example: Ten minus four equals six.
items.note: Spoken name of the subtraction symbol.

items.example: Six plus four equals ten.
items.note: Used to read an equals sign or describe an equality.

items.example: Seven times eight is fifty-six.
items.note: Common way to say multiplication of two numbers.

items.example: Nine multiplied by five is forty-five.
items.note: Alternative to times in arithmetic; not usually used for physical dimensions.

items.example: Twelve divided by three equals four.
items.note: Spoken expression for division.

items.example: The ratio may be read as five over eight.
items.note: Used to read numerator and denominator across a fraction bar.

items.example: Subtract forty-one from ninety-three to get fifty-two.
items.note: The number being subtracted comes before from; the starting number comes after it.

sectionsChecked: A: Pronunciation of numbers, fractions, decimals, percentages and measurements
B: Two-dimensional shapes and geometry vocabulary
D: Arithmetic symbols and spoken expressions
